claim: The Mecp2+/- mouse model recapitulates many phenotypes of patients with Rett syndrome (RTT), including learning and memory deficits.
source: The Mecp2+/- mouse model recapitulates many phenotypes of patients with Rett syndrome (RTT), including learning and memory deficits.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature establishing the mouse model.

claim: Place cells in RTT mice are impaired in their experience-dependent increase of spatial information.
source: We found that place cells in RTT mice are impaired in their experience-dependent increase of spatial information.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing spatial information of place cells between novel and familiar environments in RTT vs WT mice.

claim: Place cells in RTT mice show an enhanced baseline firing synchrony within ripple oscillations during rest.
source: This impairment is accompanied by an enhanced baseline firing synchrony of place cells within ripple oscillations during rest, which consequently occludes the increase in synchrony after a novel experience.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements of coactivity within ripple events during Pre-run sessions.

claim: The enhanced baseline synchrony in RTT mice occludes the increase in synchrony after a novel experience.
source: This impairment is accompanied by an enhanced baseline firing synchrony of place cells within ripple oscillations during rest, which consequently occludes the increase in synchrony after a novel experience.
evidence: This claim is supported by data showing lack of increase in coactivity from Pre-run to Post-run in RTT mice.

claim: Contextual memory is normal at short but not long time scale in RTT mice.
source: Behaviorally, contextual memory is normal at short but not long time scale in RTT mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by fear conditioning data showing similar freezing at 20 min but reduced freezing at 24 hr in RTT mice compared to WT.

claim: Hypersynchrony interferes with memory consolidation and leads to impaired spatial memory codes in RTT mice.
source: Our results suggest that hypersynchrony interferes with memory consolidation and leads to impaired spatial memory codes in RTT mice, providing a possible circuit mechanism for memory deficits in Rett Syndrome.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the combined findings of hypersynchrony, impaired experience-dependent changes, and behavioral deficits.

claim: Rett syndrome is characterized by a period of normal development lasting until 6–18 months of life, followed by a period of regression and development of motor deficits, autonomic dysfunction, and intellectual disability.
source: Rett syndrome, a postnatal neurodevelopmental disorder, is characterized by a period of normal development lasting until 6–18 months of life, followed by a period of regression and development of motor deficits, autonomic dysfunction, and intellectual disability (Chahrour and Zoghbi, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to established literature on Rett syndrome.

claim: Rett syndrome is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the X-linked gene MECP2.
source: Rett syndrome is caused by loss-of- function mutations in the X-linked gene MECP2, which encodes Methyl-CpG Binding Protein 2, a protein proposed to regulate chromatin states (Amir et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the original discovery paper.

claim: MECP2 encodes Methyl-CpG Binding Protein 2, a protein proposed to regulate chromatin states.
source: Rett syndrome is caused by loss-of- function mutations in the X-linked gene MECP2, which encodes Methyl-CpG Binding Protein 2, a protein proposed to regulate chromatin states (Amir et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation and represents established knowledge about MECP2 function.

claim: Rett syndrome is primarily seen in heterozygous females.
source: Rett syndrome is primarily seen in heterozygous females (Chahrour and Zoghbi, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to established literature.

claim: Female mice heterozygous for the deletion of Mecp2 (Mecp2+/-) have been used to model Rett syndrome.
source: Accordingly, female mice heterozygous for the deletion of Mecp2 (Mecp2+/-; hereafter referred to as RTT mice) have been used to model the syndrome (Guy et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the original paper establishing the mouse model.

claim: RTT mice recapitulate many features of the human disorder, including the cognitive phenotypes.
source: RTT mice recapitulate many features of the human disorder, including the cognitive phenotypes (Guy et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the original characterization of the mouse model.

claim: RTT mice display deficits in contextual fear memory.
source: For example, RTT mice display deficits in contextual fear memory (Samaco et al., 2013) and spatial reference memory (Hao et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous studies.

claim: RTT mice display deficits in spatial reference memory.
source: For example, RTT mice display deficits in contextual fear memory (Samaco et al., 2013) and spatial reference memory (Hao et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous studies.

claim: The hippocampus is critical for both contextual fear memory and spatial memory.
source: The hippocampus, a key area in the brain's learning and memory circuits, is critical for both contextual fear memory (Phillips and LeDoux, 1992; Fanselow, 2000) and spatial memory (Morris et al., 1982).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature on hippocampal function.

claim: Spatial memory is thought to be encoded by hippocampal 'place cells', which fire when the animal enters one or a few locations (place fields) in an environment.
source: In particular, spatial memory is thought to be encoded by hippocampal 'place cells', which fire when the animal enters one or a few locations (place fields) in an environment (O'Keefe and Dostrovsky, 1971; Wilson and McNaughton, 1993).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to foundational studies on place cells.

claim: Place field locations are mostly stable over time and become more refined as the animal's experience in the environment increases.
source: Place field locations are mostly stable over time and become more refined as the animal's experience in the environment increases (Thompson and Best, 1990; Frank et al., 2004; Cacucci et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies on place field dynamics.

claim: Experience-dependent refinement of spatial memory code is thought to involve memory consolidation in rest periods and sleep.
source: This experience-dependent refinement of spatial memory code is thought to involve memory consolidation in rest periods and sleep (Diekelmann and Born, 2010; Walker and Stickgold, 2004), during which place cells are activated synchronously within short (~100 ms) time windows of high-frequency (100–250 Hz) oscillations, called sharp-wave ripples, in the local-field potentials (LFPs) of the hippocampal CA1 area (Buzsáki et al., 1992; Csicsvari et al., 2000; Buzsáki, 1989; Wilson and McNaughton, 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature on memory consolidation.

claim: Place cells are activated synchronously within short (~100 ms) time windows of high-frequency (100–250 Hz) oscillations, called sharp-wave ripples, in the local-field potentials (LFPs) of the hippocampal CA1 area during rest periods and sleep.
source: This experience-dependent refinement of spatial memory code is thought to involve memory consolidation in rest periods and sleep (Diekelmann and Born, 2010; Walker and Stickgold, 2004), during which place cells are activated synchronously within short (~100 ms) time windows of high-frequency (100–250 Hz) oscillations, called sharp-wave ripples, in the local-field potentials (LFPs) of the hippocampal CA1 area (Buzsáki et al., 1992; Csicsvari et al., 2000; Buzsáki, 1989; Wilson and McNaughton, 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to foundational studies on ripple oscillations.

claim: The synchronous firing in ripples is believed to induce synaptic plasticity, which transforms short-term memories to long-term memories.
source: The synchronous firing in ripples is believed to induce synaptic plasticity, which transforms short-term memories to long-term memories (Buzsáki, 1989; Wilson and McNaughton, 1994; Tatsuno et al., 2007; Ji and Wilson, 2007; Sirota et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to theoretical and experimental studies on ripple function.

claim: Disrupting ripples is shown to impair experience-dependent learning.
source: Consistent with this idea, disrupting ripples is shown to impair experience-dependent learning (Girardeau et al., 2009; Ego-Stengel and Wilson, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to experimental studies that disrupted ripples.

claim: Hippocampal cells in RTT mice tend to display an exaggerated level of synchrony (hypersynchrony) in vitro and in vivo.
source: In particular, our previous study shows that hippocampal cells in RTT mice tend to display an exaggerated level of synchrony (hypersynchrony) in vitro and in vivo (Lu et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: Recordings were made from the hippocampal CA1 of adult RTT mice and their wildtype (WT) littermates that were at least 3 months of age.
source: To test the hypothesis we recorded place cells and LFPs using tetrodes (Cheng and Ji, 2013), from the hippocampal CA1 of adult RTT mice and their wildtype (WT) littermates that were at least 3 months of age (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim describes the experimental methods used in the study.

claim: Animals ran back and forth (two trajectories) for food rewards on either a novel or familiar linear track, repeatedly for two sessions (Run 1, Run 2).
source: The recordings were made as animals ran back and forth (two trajectories) for food rewards on either a novel or familiar linear track, repeatedly for two sessions (Run 1, Run 2).
evidence: This claim describes the experimental behavioral task.

claim: There was a rest session before (Pre-run) and after (Post-run) the first run session in a majority of the recordings.
source: There was also a rest session before (Pre-run) and after (Post-run) the first run session in a majority of the recordings (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim describes the experimental protocol.

claim: RTT and WT mice displayed similar performance, as measured by the number of times (laps) an animal traversed a trajectory in a run session and the animal's average speed of running.
source: During the recording on both the familiar and novel tracks, RTT and WT mice displayed similar performance, as measured by the number of times (laps) an animal traversed a trajectory in a run session and the animal's average speed of running (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data shown in Figure 1C,D.

claim: No seizures were observed behaviorally and no epileptic-like activities were detected in any of the recorded LFPs.
source: We did not observe any seizures behaviorally and did not detect any epileptic-like activities in any of the recorded LFPs.
evidence: This claim is based on direct observation during the experiments.

claim: A total of 47 cells from 9 RTT mice (RTT cells) and 93 cells from 7 WT mice (WT cells) were recorded on the novel track.
source: A total of 47 cells from 9 RTT mice (RTT cells) and 93 cells from 7 WT mice (WT cells) were recorded on the novel track.
evidence: This claim reports the sample size of recorded cells.

claim: Of the cells recorded on the novel track, 39 RTT cells and 84 WT cells were classified as putative pyramidal cells (with mean firing rate <7 Hz).
source: Of these, 39 RTT cells and 84 WT cells were classified as putative pyramidal cells (with mean firing rate <7 Hz; Table 1).
evidence: This claim describes the cell classification criteria and results.

claim: The percentage of run-active cells among all putative pyramidal cells in RTT mice (79%, N = 31) did not significantly differ from that in WT (63%, N = 53) mice (p=0.069, binomial test) on the novel track.
source: The percentage of run-active cells among all putative pyramidal cells in RTT mice (79%, N = 31) did not significantly differ from that in WT (63%, N = 53) mice (p=0.069, binomial test).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the data.

claim: The median firing rate of the run-active cells in RTT mice (median [25–75%] range: 1.8 [0.71 3.2] Hz, N = 31) was not significantly different from that in WT mice (1.1 [0.57 2.3] Hz, N = 53; p=0.10, Wilcoxon ranksum test) on the novel track.
source: The median firing rate of the run-active cells in RTT mice (median [25–75%] range: 1.8 [0.71 3.2] Hz, N = 31) was also not significantly different from that in WT mice (1.1 [0.57 2.3] Hz, N = 53; p=0.10, Wilcoxon ranksum test) on the novel track.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of firing rate data.

claim: RTT and WT cells fired spikes at specific locations (place fields) along a trajectory on the novel track.
source: On the novel track, raster plots and rate curves show that RTT and WT cells fired spikes at specific locations (place fields) along a trajectory (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by visual inspection of raster plots and rate curves shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The spatial information of RTT cells was similar to that of WT cells on the novel track.
source: We found that the spatial information of RTT cells was similar to that of WT cells (Figure 2B) on the novel track.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical comparison shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The stability of RTT cells on the novel track was significantly reduced from that of WT cells.
source: We found that the stability of RTT cells on the novel track was significantly reduced from that of WT cells (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical comparison shown in Figure 2B (p=0.0008).

claim: There was a greater number of place fields per cell per active trajectory in RTT (median [25–75%] range: 2 [1 3]; N = 31 cells) than that in WT cells (1 [1 2], N = 53; p=0.049, Wilcoxon ranksum test) on the novel track.
source: We found a greater number of place fields per cell per active trajectory in RTT (median [25–75%] range: 2 [1 3]; N = 31 cells) than that in WT cells (1 [1 2], N = 53; p=0.049, Wilcoxon ranksum test), but the place field length in RTT mice was shorter (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of place field properties.

claim: The place field length in RTT mice was shorter than in WT mice on the novel track.
source: We found a greater number of place fields per cell per active trajectory in RTT (median [25–75%] range: 2 [1 3]; N = 31 cells) than that in WT cells (1 [1 2], N = 53; p=0.049, Wilcoxon ranksum test), but the place field length in RTT mice was shorter (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical comparison shown in Figure 2B (p=0.0001).

claim: The median peak firing rate within place fields was comparable between RTT and WT cells on the novel track.
source: The median peak firing rate within place fields was comparable between RTT and WT cells on the novel track (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical comparison shown in Figure 2B (p=0.25).

claim: Place cells in RTT mice contained similar information on the novel track as those in WT mice, but encoded space by more place fields with shorter lengths.
source: These quantifications show that place cells in RTT mice contained similar information on the novel track as those in WT mice, but encoded space by more place fields with shorter lengths.
evidence: This claim summarizes the findings from the place field analysis on the novel track.

claim: 171 cells from 8 RTT mice and 136 cells from 7 WT mice were recorded on the familiar track.
source: We next performed the same analyses on RTT and WT cells active on the familiar track (Figure 2C), where we recorded 171 cells from 8 RTT mice and 136 cells from 7 WT mice.
evidence: This claim reports the sample size of recorded cells on the familiar track.

claim: Among cells recorded on the familiar track, 135 RTT cells and 102 WT cells were putative pyramidal cells.
source: Among these, 135 RTT cells and 102 WT cells were putative pyramidal cells (Table 1).
evidence: This claim describes the cell classification results on the familiar track.

claim: The percentage of run-active cells among all putative pyramidal neurons in RTT mice (77%, N = 103) was greater than that in WT (64%, N = 65) mice (p=0.035) on the familiar track.
source: The percentage of run-active cells among all putative pyramidal neurons in RTT mice (77%, N = 103) was greater than that in WT (64%, N = 65) mice (p=0.035).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the proportion of run-active cells.

claim: The median firing rate of run-active neurons in RTT (1.8 [1.1 3.0] Hz, N = 103) mice was significantly increased from that in WT mice (1.1 [0.6 2.1] Hz, N = 65; p=0.0012) on the familiar track.
source: The median firing rate of these run-active neurons in RTT (1.8 [1.1 3.0] Hz, N = 103) mice was significantly increased from that in WT mice (1.1 [0.6 2.1] Hz, N = 65; p=0.0012).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of firing rate data.

claim: The spatial information of run-active RTT cells was significantly reduced (by 63%), compared to that of WT run-active cells, on the familiar track.
source: However, the spatial information of run-active RTT cells was significantly reduced (by 63%), compared to that of WT run-active cells, while the stability was similar (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical comparison shown in Figure 2D (p=0.016).

claim: The stability of run-active RTT cells was similar to that of WT cells on the familiar track.
source: However, the spatial information of run-active RTT cells was significantly reduced (by 63%), compared to that of WT run-active cells, while the stability was similar (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical comparison shown in Figure 2D (p=0.33).

claim: The number of place fields per cell was similar between RTT (2 [1 2], N = 103 cells) and WT (1 [1 2], N = 65) cells (p=0.16, Wilcoxon ranksum test) on the familiar track.
source: The number of place fields per cell was similar between RTT (2 [1 2], N = 103 cells) and WT (1 [1 2], N = 65) cells (p=0.16, Wilcoxon ranksum test) on the familiar track, but the place field length of RTT cells was significantly larger than that of WT cells (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of place field properties.

claim: The place field length of RTT cells was significantly larger than that of WT cells on the familiar track.
source: The number of place fields per cell was similar between RTT (2 [1 2], N = 103 cells) and WT (1 [1 2], N = 65) cells (p=0.16, Wilcoxon ranksum test) on the familiar track, but the place field length of RTT cells was significantly larger than that of WT cells (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical comparison shown in Figure 2D (p=2.1×10−8).

claim: The median peak firing rate within place fields was comparable between RTT and WT cells on the familiar track.
source: The median peak firing rate within place fields was comparable between RTT and WT cells (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical comparison shown in Figure 2D (p=0.26).

claim: The reduced specificity of RTT cells on the familiar track was due to larger place fields.
source: The results suggest that the reduced specificity of RTT cells on the familiar track was due to larger place fields.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the combined findings of reduced spatial information and larger place fields.

claim: In WT mice, the median spatial information of place cells was greatly increased (300%) from the novel to familiar track (p=3.3×10−16, Wilcoxon ranksum test).
source: In WT mice, the median spatial information of place cells was greatly increased (300%) from the novel to familiar track (p=3.3×10−16, Wilcoxon ranksum test), indicating an experience-dependent refinement of firing specificity in WT cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical comparison of spatial information between novel and familiar tracks in WT mice.

claim: The increase in spatial information from novel to familiar track in WT mice indicates an experience-dependent refinement of firing specificity in WT cells.
source: In WT mice, the median spatial information of place cells was greatly increased (300%) from the novel to familiar track (p=3.3×10−16, Wilcoxon ranksum test), indicating an experience-dependent refinement of firing specificity in WT cells.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the observed increase in spatial information.

claim: In WT mice, the number of place fields remained similar between the novel and familiar track.
source: The number of place fields remained similar between the novel and familiar track, but the field length became significantly smaller (p=0.00056) and median peak firing rate within place fields was significantly increased (p=1.5×10−7).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical comparison of place field properties between novel and familiar tracks in WT mice.

claim: In WT mice, the field length became significantly smaller from novel to familiar track (p=0.00056).
source: The number of place fields remained similar between the novel and familiar track, but the field length became significantly smaller (p=0.00056) and median peak firing rate within place fields was significantly increased (p=1.5×10−7).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical comparison of place field length.

claim: In WT mice, median peak firing rate within place fields was significantly increased from novel to familiar track (p=1.5×10−7).
source: The number of place fields remained similar between the novel and familiar track, but the field length became significantly smaller (p=0.00056) and median peak firing rate within place fields was significantly increased (p=1.5×10−7).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical comparison of peak firing rates.

claim: Experience refines place cells by narrowing place field sizes and increasing firing rates in WT mice.
source: The result suggests that experience refines place cells by narrowing place field sizes and increasing firing rates.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the observed changes in place field properties with experience in WT mice.

claim: In RTT mice, the spatial information of RTT cells was only modestly increased between novel and familiar tracks (48%, p=0.008).
source: In RTT mice, the spatial information of RTT cells was only modestly increased between novel and familiar tracks (48%, p=0.008), indicating a reduction in experience-dependent refinement of firing specificity in RTT mice, compared to that in WT mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical comparison of spatial information between novel and familiar tracks in RTT mice.

claim: The modest increase in spatial information in RTT mice indicates a reduction in experience-dependent refinement of firing specificity in RTT mice, compared to that in WT mice.
source: In RTT mice, the spatial information of RTT cells was only modestly increased between novel and familiar tracks (48%, p=0.008), indicating a reduction in experience-dependent refinement of firing specificity in RTT mice, compared to that in WT mice.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation comparing the experience-dependent changes between RTT and WT mice.

claim: In RTT mice, the number of place fields was similar between the novel and familiar track.
source: The number of place fields was similar between the novel and familiar track and the peak rate increased (p=4.5×10−5), as in WT mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of place field numbers between novel and familiar tracks in RTT mice.

claim: In RTT mice, the peak rate increased from novel to familiar track (p=4.5×10−5), as in WT mice.
source: The number of place fields was similar between the novel and familiar track and the peak rate increased (p=4.5×10−5), as in WT mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical comparison of peak firing rates.

claim: Place fields in RTT mice were relatively narrow on the novel track and became significantly widened on the familiar track (p=2.4×10−8).
source: However, place fields in RTT mice were relatively narrow on the novel track and became significantly widened on the familiar track (p=2.4×10−8).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical comparison of place field lengths between novel and familiar tracks in RTT mice.

claim: Although place cells in RTT mice still increased spatial information with experience, likely due to higher peak firing rates, this increase was much less than that in WT mice mainly because of larger place fields.
source: The comparison indicates that, although place cells in RTT mice still increased spatial information with experience, likely due to higher peak firing rates, this increase was much less than that in WT mice mainly because of larger place fields.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the combined findings on experience-dependent changes in RTT vs WT mice.

claim: The downsampling analysis showed that 42% of the iterations produced a significant difference in spatial information between WT and RTT cells on the familiar track and 3% on the novel track.
source: We found that 42% of the iterations produced a significant difference in spatial information between WT and RTT cells on the familiar track and 3% in spatial information on the novel track (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim reports the results of the downsampling analysis.

claim: 98% of the downsampling iterations produced a significant difference in spatial information of WT cells between the novel and familiar tracks, but only 25% in RTT cells.
source: On the other hand, 98% of the iterations produced a significant difference in spatial information of WT cells between the novel and familiar tracks, but only 25% in RTT cells, suggesting that the experience-dependent refinement was robust in WT mice, but largely disappeared in RTT mice, with the downsampled cells.
evidence: This claim reports the results of the downsampling analysis comparing novel vs familiar tracks.

claim: The experience-dependent refinement was robust in WT mice, but largely disappeared in RTT mice, even with downsampled cells.
source: On the other hand, 98% of the iterations produced a significant difference in spatial information of WT cells between the novel and familiar tracks, but only 25% in RTT cells, suggesting that the experience-dependent refinement was robust in WT mice, but largely disappeared in RTT mice, with the downsampled cells.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the downsampling analysis results.

claim: On the novel track, WT and RTT cells showed similar spatial information in early and late laps during Run 1 and throughout Run 2.
source: On the novel track, WT and RTT cells showed similar spatial information in early and late laps during Run 1 and throughout Run 2.
evidence: This claim is supported by lap-by-lap analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: On the familiar track, WT cells started both Run 1 and Run 2 with already high spatial information in early laps, but RTT cells started with a low level of spatial information similar to that on the novel track.
source: On the familiar track, WT cells started both Run 1 and Run 2 with already high spatial information in early laps, but RTT cells started with a low level of spatial information similar to that on the novel track.
evidence: This claim is supported by lap-by-lap analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Place cells in RTT mice could produce specific firing from ongoing sensory experience on the track.
source: This suggests that place cells in RTT mice could produce specific firing from ongoing sensory experience on the track.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the lap-by-lap analysis showing that RTT cells can increase spatial information within a session.

claim: The specificity of place cells in RTT mice was not maintained between running sessions or across days.
source: However, the specificity was not maintained between running sessions or across days.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the finding that RTT cells start with low spatial information at the beginning of each session on the familiar track.

claim: Theta phases of both RTT and WT place cells precessed as animals passed through their place fields.
source: We found that theta phases of both RTT and WT place cells precessed as animals passed through their place fields (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by visual inspection of theta phase precession plots in Figure 3A.

claim: The linear correlation and the slope of the linear regression of theta phase precession did not significantly differ between WT and RTT cells on either the novel or the familiar track.
source: The linear correlation and the slope of the linear regression did not significantly differ between WT and RTT cells on either the novel or the familiar track (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical comparisons shown in Figure 3B.

claim: There was a small, yet significant, reduction in the circular-linear correlation of RTT cells in the familiar environment (11%), compared to that of WT cells, but not in the novel environment.
source: However, there was a small, yet significant, reduction in the circular-linear correlation of RTT cells in the familiar environment (11%), compared to that of WT cells, but not in the novel environment (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical comparison shown in Figure 3C (p=0.016 for familiar, p=0.77 for novel).

claim: The fine level of correlation between firing activity and location within place fields was present in RTT mice, but could be slightly weaker in the familiar environment, possibly related to their larger place fields.
source: The analysis suggests that the fine level of correlation between firing activity and location within place fields was present in RTT mice, but could be slightly weaker in the familiar environment, possibly related to their larger place fields.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the theta phase precession analysis results.

claim: ANOVA analysis shows that there was no significant effect of genotype or significant interaction between genotype and rest session in ripple rate, duration, amplitude, or frequency in the novel environment.
source: In the novel environment, ANOVA analysis shows that there was no significant effect of genotype or significant interaction between genotype and rest session in ripple rate, duration, amplitude, or frequency (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by ANOVA statistical analysis of ripple properties.

claim: Similar findings were made in the familiar environment regarding ripple properties.
source: Similar findings were made in the familiar environment (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by ANOVA statistical analysis of ripple properties in the familiar environment.

claim: Ripples in RTT and WT mice were qualitatively similar in rest sessions.
source: The data suggest that ripples in RTT and WT mice were qualitatively similar in rest sessions.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the ripple property analysis.

claim: In the novel room, the firing rates of all putative pyramidal cells or run-active cells were not significantly different between WT and RTT in either Pre- or Post-run.
source: In the novel room, the firing rates of all putative pyramidal cells or run-active cells were not significantly different between WT and RTT in either Pre- or Post-run.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: In the familiar room, the median firing rate of all putative pyramidal cells in RTT mice was similar to that in WT mice in both Pre-run and Post-run.
source: In the familiar room, the median firing rate of all putative pyramidal cells in RTT mice was similar to that in WT mice in both Pre-run and Post-run, but run-active cells had higher firing rate in RTT mice than in WT mice, especially in Pre-run.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: In the familiar room, run-active cells had higher firing rate in RTT mice than in WT mice, especially in Pre-run.
source: In the familiar room, the median firing rate of all putative pyramidal cells in RTT mice was similar to that in WT mice in both Pre-run and Post-run, but run-active cells had higher firing rate in RTT mice than in WT mice, especially in Pre-run.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1 (p=0.003 for Pre-run).

claim: Run-active cells in RTT mice participated in ripples with a higher rate and fired more spikes per ripple event in the familiar room, but not in the novel room.
source: Indeed, run-active cells in RTT mice participated in ripples with a higher rate and fired more spikes per ripple event in the familiar room, but not in the novel room (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Run-inactive cells did not differ between WT and RTT mice in ripple participation rate or number of spikes per ripple in either the novel or familiar room.
source: In contrast, run-inactive cells did not differ between WT and RTT mice in either of these parameters in either the novel or familiar room (Figure 4—figure supplement 3), providing a control that the difference in ripple participation between WT and RTT mice was not due to differences in resting behavior or ripple events per se.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: The lack of difference in run-inactive cells provides a control that the difference in ripple participation between WT and RTT mice was not due to differences in resting behavior or ripple events per se.
source: In contrast, run-inactive cells did not differ between WT and RTT mice in either of these parameters in either the novel or familiar room (Figure 4—figure supplement 3), providing a control that the difference in ripple participation between WT and RTT mice was not due to differences in resting behavior or ripple events per se.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the run-inactive cell analysis as a control.

claim: Place cells active in a new spatial experience tend to fire synchronously during ripples immediately after the experience more frequently than during ripples before.
source: It is known that place cells active in a new spatial experience tend to fire synchronously during ripples immediately after the experience more frequently than during ripples before (Wilson and McNaughton, 1994; Skaggs and McNaughton, 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: In WT mice, run-active cells rarely fired together during ripples in Pre-run, but did so more frequently in Post-run.
source: In WT mice, run-active cells rarely fired together during ripples in Pre-run, but did so more frequently in Post-run.
evidence: This claim is supported by visual inspection of spike rasters and cross-correlograms in Figure 5A,B.

claim: In RTT mice run-active cells already fired together in Pre-run and they appeared not to do so more frequently in Post-run.
source: However, in RTT mice run-active cells already fired together in Pre-run and they appeared not to do so more frequently in Post-run (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by visual inspection of spike rasters and cross-correlograms in Figure 5A,B.

claim: Cross-correlograms of run-active cell pairs in WT mice showed low correlation around the time lag 0 in Pre-run and relatively high correlation in Post-run.
source: Cross-correlograms of these cell pairs in WT mice showed low correlation around the time lag 0 in Pre-run and relatively high correlation in Post-run (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by visual inspection of cross-correlograms in Figure 5B.

claim: Cross-correlograms in RTT mice showed high correlation around the time lag 0 already in Pre-run, without further increase in Post-run.
source: However, cross-correlograms in RTT mice showed high correlation around the time lag 0 already in Pre-run, without further increase in Post-run (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by visual inspection of cross-correlograms in Figure 5B.

claim: The coactivity in WT mice was significantly increased from Pre- to Post-run on the novel track (p=0.044, paired Student's t-test).
source: We found that the coactivity in WT mice was significantly increased from Pre- to Post-run (Figure 5C), indicating an experience-dependent increase in synchrony following running on the novel track, as expected (Wilson and McNaughton, 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The increase in coactivity in WT mice indicates an experience-dependent increase in synchrony following running on the novel track.
source: We found that the coactivity in WT mice was significantly increased from Pre- to Post-run (Figure 5C), indicating an experience-dependent increase in synchrony following running on the novel track, as expected (Wilson and McNaughton, 1994).
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the coactivity increase in WT mice, supported by citation.

claim: In RTT mice, the coactivity was not significantly different between Pre-run and Post-run on the novel track (p=0.47).
source: In RTT mice, however, the coactivity was not significantly different between Pre-run and Post-run, indicating a lack of increase in synchrony after the novel track experience (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The lack of change in coactivity in RTT mice indicates a lack of increase in synchrony after the novel track experience.
source: In RTT mice, however, the coactivity was not significantly different between Pre-run and Post-run, indicating a lack of increase in synchrony after the novel track experience (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the coactivity results in RTT mice.

claim: The Pre-run coactivity was significantly higher in RTT mice than that in WT mice (p=0.039, Wilcoxon ranksum test).
source: Moreover, the Pre-run coactivity was significantly higher in RTT mice than that in WT mice, whereas the Post-run coactivity was not significantly different.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The Post-run coactivity was not significantly different between RTT and WT mice (p=0.65).
source: Moreover, the Pre-run coactivity was significantly higher in RTT mice than that in WT mice, whereas the Post-run coactivity was not significantly different.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Run-active cells in RTT mice failed to increase their synchrony following a novel experience and this failure appeared to be due to their higher than normal synchrony (hypersynchrony) prior to the experience.
source: Therefore, run-active cells in RTT mice failed to increase their synchrony following a novel experience and this failure appeared to be due to their higher than normal synchrony (hypersynchrony) prior to the experience, consistent with our previous study (Lu et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the coactivity results, supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The coactivity of all putative pyramidal cell pairs in RTT mice was significantly higher than that in WT mice in Pre-run before the novel-track running (p=0.0007, Wilcoxon ranksum test).
source: Indeed, we found that the coactivity in RTT mice was significantly higher than that in WT mice (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: A similar hypersynchrony among run-active cells in RTT mice, relative to those in WT mice, was found within ripples in both Pre- and Post-run in the familiar environment.
source: Second, we analyzed the coactivity of run-active cells in the familiar environment. We found a similar hypersynchrony among run-active cells in RTT mice, relative to those in WT mice, within ripples in both Pre- and Post-run (Figure 5—figure supplement 2), although the coactivity of RTT cells in Post-run now became significantly higher than that in Pre-run, likely because the repetitive experience on the familiar track eventually further increased the cells' coactivity (see Discussion).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The coactivity of RTT cells in Post-run became significantly higher than that in Pre-run in the familiar environment, likely because the repetitive experience on the familiar track eventually further increased the cells' coactivity.
source: We found a similar hypersynchrony among run-active cells in RTT mice, relative to those in WT mice, within ripples in both Pre- and Post-run (Figure 5—figure supplement 2), although the coactivity of RTT cells in Post-run now became significantly higher than that in Pre-run, likely because the repetitive experience on the familiar track eventually further increased the cells' coactivity (see Discussion).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis and includes a speculative interpretation.

claim: The coactivity of run-silent cells within ripples was higher in RTT mice than that in WT mice (p=0.017).
source: Finally, we computed the coactivity of run-silent cells within ripples (Pre- and Post-run in novel and familiar environments combined) and found that the coactivity was higher in RTT mice than that in WT mice (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: The results suggest a general hypersynchrony among CA1 neurons in RTT mice.
source: The results suggest a general hypersynchrony among CA1 neurons in RTT mice.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the combined coactivity analyses across different cell types.

claim: Previous studies have shown that RTT mice are impaired in contextual fear memory when they are tested 3 or 24 hr after learning.
source: Previous studies have shown that RTT mice are impaired in contextual fear memory when they are tested 3 or 24 hr after learning (Samaco et al., 2013; Hao et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The freezing level at 20 min was comparable between RTT and WT mice (p=0.78, Wilcoxon ranksum test).
source: We found that the freezing level at 20 min was comparable between RTT and WT mice (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: ANOVA analysis revealed a significant effect of genotype on freezing level (F(1,66) = 4.2; p=0.044).
source: ANOVA analysis revealed a significant effect of genotype and post-hoc Wilcoxon ranksum test showed that there was a significant difference at 24 hr, but not at 20 min, between WT and RTT mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by ANOVA statistical analysis of freezing data.

claim: Post-hoc Wilcoxon ranksum test showed that there was a significant difference in freezing at 24 hr (p=0.034), but not at 20 min (p=0.78), between WT and RTT mice.
source: ANOVA analysis revealed a significant effect of genotype and post-hoc Wilcoxon ranksum test showed that there was a significant difference at 24 hr, but not at 20 min, between WT and RTT mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by post-hoc statistical analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The contextual memory at a short time scale (20 min) was relatively normal in RTT mice.
source: Nevertheless, our data did show that the contextual memory at a short time scale (20 min) was relatively normal in RTT mice.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the fear conditioning results at 20 min.

claim: The finding that contextual memory is normal at short time scale but impaired at longer time scales is consistent with a memory consolidation impairment in RTT mice.
source: This result, together with previous studies (Samaco et al., 2013; Hao et al., 2015) showing contextual fear memory deficits at longer time scales, is consistent with a memory consolidation impairment in RTT mice.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation combining current and previous findings, supported by citations.

claim: CA1 place cells in RTT mice contain a similar amount of spatial information as those in WT mice on the novel track, but form more place fields with relatively shorter field lengths.
source: Our data show that CA1 place cells in RTT mice contain a similar amount of spatial information as those in WT mice on the novel track, but form more place fields with relatively shorter field lengths.
evidence: This claim summarizes the findings on place cell properties on the novel track.

claim: Ongoing sensory input is capable of driving place cells to encode novel spatial experience in RTT mice.
source: This suggests that, although certain aspects of the encoding are changed, ongoing sensory input is capable of driving place cells to encode novel spatial experience in RTT mice.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the finding that RTT cells have similar spatial information on the novel track.

claim: Contextual fear memory in RTT mice is normal shortly after learning, presumably because place cells in RTT mice can initially encode the spatial context of a conditioning box.
source: Indeed, our data show that contextual fear memory in RTT mice is normal shortly after learning, presumably because place cells in RTT mice can initially encode the spatial context of a conditioning box.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation linking the place cell findings to the behavioral results.

claim: Place cells in WT mice are more specific on the familiar track with narrower place fields and increased peak firing rates, compared to those on the novel track.
source: Our data also show that place cells in WT mice are more specific on the familiar track with narrower place fields and increased peak firing rates, compared to those on the novel track.
evidence: This claim summarizes the findings on experience-dependent changes in WT mice.

claim: Place cells in RTT mice increase their spatial specificity from the novel to the familiar track much less than those in WT mice.
source: In contrast, place cells in RTT mice increase their spatial specificity from the novel to the familiar track much less than those in WT mice.
evidence: This claim summarizes the findings on impaired experience-dependent changes in RTT mice.

claim: The key finding of impaired increase in spatial information of RTT cells in the familiar environment is robust even with downsampled cells.
source: Consistent with this observation, RTT mice are impaired in contextual fear memories tested 3 or 24 hr after learning in previous studies (Samaco et al., 2013; Hao et al., 2015). Therefore, abnormal spatial memory code refinement may underlie behavioral deficits in RTT mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by the downsampling analysis and citations to previous behavioral studies.

claim: Abnormal spatial memory code refinement may underlie behavioral deficits in RTT mice.
source: Therefore, abnormal spatial memory code refinement may underlie behavioral deficits in RTT mice.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation linking the neural findings to behavioral deficits.

claim: Ripple events are important in memory processing.
source: It is known that ripple evens are important in memory processing (Girardeau et al., 2009; Ego-Stengel and Wilson, 2010; Wu et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: The hypersynchrony during Pre-run in RTT mice may be related to the greater number of place fields or shorter field size seen on the novel track, but appears not sufficient to impact overall spatial information or the behavioral performance.
source: This hypersynchrony may be related to the greater number of place fields or shorter field size seen on the novel track, but appears not sufficient to impact overall spatial information or the behavioral performance.
evidence: This claim is a speculative interpretation of the relationship between hypersynchrony and place field properties.

claim: The experience-dependent increase in firing synchrony is hypothesized to be a neural mechanism for memory consolidation, because it likely results from synaptic plasticity during the novel experience and leads to further experience-specific synaptic plasticity for memory consolidation.
source: This experience-dependent increase in firing synchrony is hypothesized to be a neural mechanism for memory consolidation, because it likely results from synaptic plasticity during the novel experience and leads to further experience-specific synaptic plasticity for memory consolidation (Buzsáki, 1989; Wilson and McNaughton, 1994), via precise 'replay' of the activity patterns associated with the experience (Skaggs and McNaughton, 1996; Lee and Wilson, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to theoretical and experimental literature.

claim: The finding that experience-dependent increase in synchrony is reduced in RTT mice suggests an impairment in memory consolidation in these animals.
source: Our finding that this experience-dependent increase in synchrony is reduced in RTT mice suggests an impairment in memory consolidation in these animals.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the coactivity findings.

claim: Place fields are relatively unstable between two running sessions of the novel track in RTT mice, providing further evidence that spatial memory codes fail to consolidate following the first running session.
source: In addition, we also found that place fields are relatively unstable between two running sessions of the novel track, providing further evidence that spatial memory codes fail to consolidate following the first running session.
evidence: This claim is supported by the stability analysis and is interpreted as evidence for consolidation failure.

claim: The baseline hypersynchrony occludes further experience-dependent increases in firing synchrony and thus prevents the experience-specific synaptic plasticity underlying memory consolidation, possibly due to saturation or other homeostatic mechanisms.
source: Given that there is hypersynchony during Pre-run in RTT mice, it is likely that this baseline hypersynchrony occludes further experience-dependent increases in firing synchrony and thus prevents the experience-specific synaptic plasticity underlying memory consolidation, possibly due to saturation or other homeostatic mechanisms.
evidence: This claim is a speculative interpretation of the mechanism underlying the observed deficits.

claim: The hypersynchrony, as well as memory deficits, in RTT mice can be rescued by deep-brain stimulation that promotes synaptic plasticity.
source: Our previous study also showed that the hypersynchrony, as well as memory deficits, in RTT mice can be rescued by deep-brain stimulation that promotes synaptic plasticity (Hao et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Although sensory input can drive the initial formation of spatial memory codes in novel environments, the baseline hypersynchrony leads to reduced experience-dependent increase in firing synchrony within ripples and consequently impairs memory consolidation and memory code refinement.
source: Taken together with these previous findings, our data support a model that, although sensory input can drive the initial formation of spatial memory codes in novel environments, the baseline hypersynchrony leads to reduced experience-dependent increase in firing synchrony within ripples and consequently impairs memory consolidation and memory code refinement.
evidence: This claim is a synthesis of the current findings with previous work into a proposed model.

claim: In WT mice, although there is still an increase in firing synchrony after running on a familiar track, the increase is less dramatic than that following running on a novel track, likely because experience-induced firing synchrony among run-active cells gets weaker when memories no longer need to be consolidated.
source: In WT mice, although there is still an increase in firing synchrony after running on a familiar track, the increase is less dramatic than that following running on a novel track. This is likely because experience-induced firing synchrony among run-active cells gets weaker when memories no longer need to be consolidated.
evidence: This claim is a speculative interpretation of the coactivity changes in WT mice on the familiar track.

claim: In RTT mice, although hypersynchrony is still present in the rest session before running on the familiar track, the hypersynchrony among run-active cells becomes less prominent than that before running on the novel track.
source: In RTT mice, although hypersynchrony is still present in the rest session before running on the familiar track, the hypersynchrony among run-active cells becomes less prominent than that before running on the novel track.
evidence: This claim is an observation from the coactivity analysis comparing novel and familiar tracks in RTT mice.

claim: Running on the familiar track induces a larger increase in the firing synchrony than running on the novel track in RTT mice.
source: Also, running on the familiar track induces a larger increase in the firing synchrony than running on the novel track.
evidence: This claim is an observation from the coactivity analysis in RTT mice.

claim: Run-active cells in RTT mice exhibit a change following the running on the familiar track similar to the cells in WT mice following the running on the novel track.
source: It seems that run-active cells in RTT mice exhibit a change following the running on the familiar track similar to the cells in WT mice following the running on the novel track.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation comparing the patterns of coactivity changes between RTT and WT mice.

claim: The repetitive overtraining experience on the familiar track may induce some long-term synaptic plasticity that 'breaks' the baseline hypersynchrony in RTT mice.
source: One possibility is that this is caused by the repetitive overtraining experience on the familiar track, which may induce some long-term synaptic plasticity that 'breaks' the baseline hypersynchrony.
evidence: This claim is a speculative interpretation of the coactivity changes on the familiar track in RTT mice.

claim: The low baseline coactivity in RTT mice on the familiar track may permit some experience-dependent increase in firing synchrony within ripples.
source: The low baseline may now permit some experience-dependent increase in firing synchrony within ripples.
evidence: This claim is a speculative interpretation of the mechanism allowing increased coactivity on the familiar track.

claim: The notion of abnormal memory consolidation caused by abnormal firing synchrony within ripples in RTT mice is consistent with a previous study on a mouse model of schizophrenia, which found that stronger correlations of place cell pairs within ripples lead to impaired reactivation of place cell patterns following an experience.
source: Our notion of abnormal memory consolidation caused by abnormal firing synchrony within ripples in RTT mice is consistent with a previous study on a mouse model of schizophrenia, which found that stronger correlations of place cell pairs within ripples lead to impaired reactivation of place cell patterns following an experience (Suh et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim compares the current findings to a previous study, supported by citation.

claim: In the current study, the abnormally high correlation occurs prior to any experience, and therefore the abnormal memory consolidation appears to be caused by a baseline hypersynchrony within ripples during resting.
source: However, in our study the abnormally high correlation occurs prior to any experience, and therefore the abnormal memory consolidation appears to be caused by a baseline hypersynchrony within ripples during resting.
evidence: This claim distinguishes the current findings from the previous schizophrenia study.

claim: The idea that abnormal place field refinement in RTT mice is linked to abnormal neuronal activities within ripples is supported by a recent study that silencing place cells within ripples impairs refinement of their place fields.
source: In addition, our idea that abnormal place field refinement in RTT mice is linked to abnormal neuronal activities within ripples is supported by a recent study that silencing place cells within ripples impairs refinement of their place fields (Roux et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a recent study.

claim: The finding of unstable place fields on the novel track in the face of hypersynchrony within ripples is consistent with several papers that study how manipulating neuronal activities within ripples affects place field stability.
source: Finally, our finding of unstable place fields on the novel track in the face of hypersynchrony within ripples is consistent with several papers that study how manipulating neuronal activities within ripples affects place field stability.
evidence: This claim relates the current findings to previous studies on ripple manipulation.

claim: Silencing place cells within ripples leads to unstable place fields of these cells.
source: Silencing place cells within ripples leads to unstable place fields of these cells (Roux et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Disrupting ripples altogether did not impact place field stability in one study, but did reduce stability of a portion of place cells in another study.
source: Disrupting ripples altogether did not impact place field stability in one study (Kovács et al., 2016), but did reduce stability of a portion of place cells in another study (van de Ven et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to two previous studies with different findings.

claim: Place cell silencing or ripple disruption is a much more severe alteration than the hypersynchrony in RTT mice, yet the hypersynchrony in RTT mice seems sufficient to impact place field stability.
source: In any case, place cell silencing or ripple disruption is a much more severe alteration than the hypersynchrony in RTT mice, yet the hypersynchrony in RTT mice seems sufficient to impact place field stability.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation comparing the severity of different manipulations and their effects.

claim: The RTT mouse model shares the same genetic deficiencies that cause Rett syndrome and recapitulates key behavioral deficits in Rett patients, including impaired learning and memory.
source: The RTT mouse model shares the same genetic deficiencies that cause Rett syndrome and recapitulates key behavioral deficits in Rett patients, including impaired learning and memory (Samaco et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work validating the mouse model.

claim: It is likely that the in vivo neural circuit deficits identified in RTT mice may also occur in human patients.
source: It is likely that the in vivo neural circuit deficits identified here in RTT mice may also occur in human patients.
evidence: This claim is a speculative extrapolation from the mouse model to human patients.

claim: There is evidence that the increased synchrony described in RTT mice is paralleled by human studies of Rett patients using fMRI or EEG recordings, which have shown that hypersynchronous neural activity at baseline is a hallmark of the disease.
source: Indeed, there is evidence that the increased synchrony described here is paralleled by human studies of Rett patients using fMRI or EEG recordings, which have shown that hypersynchronous neural activity at baseline is a hallmark of the disease (Naidu et al., 2001; Garofalo et al., 1988; Glaze, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to human studies on Rett patients.

claim: Baseline hypersynchrony in RTT mice reduces experience-dependent increase in firing synchrony for memory consolidation and consequently leads to impaired spatial memory codes.
source: Our data suggest that baseline hypersynchrony in RTT mice reduces experience-dependent increase in firing synchrony for memory consolidation and consequently leads to impaired spatial memory codes.
evidence: This claim is a summary of the proposed mechanism based on the study's findings.

claim: The animal study on RTT mice suggests that abnormal memory codes caused by impaired memory consolidation underlie the cognitive deficits in Rett syndrome.
source: Our animal study on RTT mice thus suggests that abnormal memory codes caused by impaired memory consolidation underlie the cognitive deficits in Rett syndrome.
evidence: This claim is a concluding interpretation extrapolating from the mouse model to the human disease.
